summary: The process in RFC 6761 for registering special-use domain names has run into unexpected difficulties in practice. This memo lists the problems found so far in an attempt to be comprehensive, and discusses what needs to be addressed.

plainLanguage.summary: Some protocols need their own corner of the domain name space, such as the name used for devices on a home network. There is a formal process for reserving such a name, and this document lists the problems that came up when people tried to follow it.

questions: why is special-use domain name registration difficult
what problems does the special-use domain name registry have
how does a domain name get reserved for technical use
subtitle: When a process for reserving special domain names breaks down

tldr.problem: The rulebook for reserving domain names for technical use turned out to be harder to apply than expected, and the IETF had to review it.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists twenty-one problems found in practice, describes the documents and history behind the process, and explains how names reach the root of the domain namespace without going through it.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement: solutions and their costs were explicitly left out of scope, and the document takes no position on which problems are real or who should fix them.

today: RFC 8244 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the DNSOP working group's review of the RFC 6761 process. It is a problem statement: solutions and their costs were explicitly left to a separate document, and the text notes that it is required reading for IETF participants who want to express an informed opinion on the topic.

sections.title: Why the Process Was Reviewed
sections.content:
One of the key services required to use the Internet is name resolution, the process of translating a symbolic name into some object or set of objects to which the name refers, most typically one or more IP addresses. These names are often called domain names, but care must be taken not to assume that the term implies the use of the Domain Name System for resolving them.

RFC 6761 created the Special-Use Domain Names registry maintained by IANA, defined policies for adding to the registry, and made suggestions about how those policies might be implemented. Since its publication the IETF has been asked to designate several new Special-Use Domain Names in this registry, and during the evaluation process for them it encountered several different sorts of issues. As a result the IETF decided to investigate the problem and decide if and how the process defined in RFC 6761 can be improved, or whether it should be deprecated. The DNSOP Working Group charter was extended to include a review of the process, and this document is a product of that review.

Based on current ICANN and IETF practice, there are several different types of names in the root of the Domain Namespace: names reserved by the IETF for technical purposes; names assigned by ICANN to the public DNS root, some of which may be names the IETF reserved for technical purposes appearing in the global DNS root for reasons pertaining to the operation of the DNS; ICANN Reserved Names, which may not be applied for as top-level domains; names used by other organisations without following established processes; and names that are unused and available for assignment to one of the previous categories.

The document presents a list, derived from a variety of sources including discussion in the DNSOP Working Group, of the problems associated with the assignment of Special-Use Domain Names. The list is intended to be an unfiltered compilation of issues. It also includes descriptions of existing practice as it relates to the use of domain names, a brief history of domain names, and some observations by participants who have experience with the current situation.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Architecture Board asked the DNS working group to look again at how names are reserved for technical use, because the attempts to use the existing rulebook had been slow and had produced surprises. This document is the result of that look.

sections.title: The Words Used
sections.content:
The document uses the terminology from RFC 7719 and defines three terms of its own. A Domain Name is used as defined in Section 2 of RFC 7719. The Domain Namespace is the set of all possible domain names. A Special-Use Domain Name is a domain name listed in the Special-Use Domain Names registry.

It also expands four abbreviations. IANA is the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. ICANN is the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers. TLD is Top-Level Domain, as defined in RFC 7719. gTLD is Generic Top-Level Domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The document separates three ideas that are often run together: a domain name as a string of labels, the whole set of all possible such strings, and the subset that has been officially marked as special.

sections.title: The Twenty-One Problems
sections.content:
The list has two goals: to enumerate all the problems that Special-Use Domain Names are a solution to, and to enumerate all the problems raised in the process of trying to use RFC 6761 as intended. As some may fall into both categories, no attempt is made to categorise them. There is a broad diversity of opinion about the set, and not every participant agrees that each enumerated problem is actually a problem; the document takes no position on the relative validity of the problems, nor on the organisation responsible for addressing each one. It only enumerates them, provides context for thinking about them, and provides a context for future discussion of solutions. The list is not in order of importance: numbers are assigned so each problem can be referenced, not to indicate priority.

The first four problems concern authority and coordination. Although the IETF and ICANN have a liaison relationship through which special-use allocations can be discussed, there is no formal process for coordinating these allocations, and the lack of coordination complicates management of the root of the Domain Namespace and could lead to conflicts in name assignments. There is no explicit scoping as to what can constitute a technical use, and no consensus within the IETF as to what the term means. Not all developers of Internet protocols agree that authority over the entire Domain Namespace should reside solely with the IETF and ICANN. And although those two organisations nominally have authority, neither can enforce it over a third party that simply starts using a subset of the namespace, which may observe that the IETF has never asserted control over what protocols are allowed and that the principle of permissionless innovation suggests there should be a way for people to include new uses of domain names in new protocols and applications.

Problem 5 records that organisations do sometimes use subsets of the Domain Namespace without following established processes, and lists seven reasons a third party might do so: lack of knowledge that a process exists; the intended use being covered by the generic top-level domain process but with no such process ongoing; the intended use being covered by that process but the third party not wanting to pay a fee; the intended use being covered by an IETF process but the third party not wanting to follow it; the intended use being covered by an ICANN or IETF process but the third party expecting refusal or non-action; lack of knowledge that a name intended only for local use may nevertheless leak; and lack of knowledge that a name used locally with informal allocation may subsequently be allocated formally, creating operational problems.

Problems 6 and 7 concern resolution. There is demand for more than one name resolution protocol for domain names, but domain names contain no metadata saying which protocol to use, and name resolution APIs give no way to specify one. And when a Special-Use Domain Name is added to the registry, not all software that processes such names will understand the special use, so in many cases resolution software will use the DNS for names not known to have a special use. Such use results in queries for Special-Use Domain Names being sent to DNS authoritative servers, which may constitute an operational problem for operators of root zone servers and may inadvertently reveal private information through the contents of the query.

Problems 8 to 10 describe resistance and slowness. Some protocol developers assumed they could not succeed in getting a name assigned through the RFC 6761 process because, when the IETF has tried to follow it, it has been slow and uncertain: assigning the first new name, .local, took more than ten years from beginning to end, longer by a factor of ten than any other part of the protocol development process, largely because those ten years included time to develop the process as well as use it. There is also strong resistance within the IETF to assigning domain names to resolution systems outside the DNS, for seven listed reasons: it requires a mechanism for identifying which resolution process a name needs; assertion of authority, so that someone who claims a name without following the process should suffer a consequence; more than one name resolution protocol being bad because a single protocol is less complicated to implement and deploy; alternative protocols having different semantics, since DNS has record types that others may not support; a free IETF process becoming an alternative to the more costly route of registering through ICANN; a name assigned for a particular purpose when a more general use would be more beneficial; and the risk of the IETF becoming embroiled in an expensive dispute with parties who believe a name belongs to them. If there were no process for assigning names for technical use through the IETF, there is a concern that protocols needing such names would not be able to get them.

Problems 11 to 18 concern the process itself. In some cases where the IETF has made assignments through the RFC 6761 process, technical mistakes have been made through misunderstandings of what the process specifies, such as treating the list of suggested considerations as requirements that all must be met; in other cases the IETF has made de facto assignments without following the process at all. Several top-level domain names are in use without due process for a variety of purposes, and their status needs to be clarified and recorded to avoid future disputes. In principle the process could be used to document the existence of domain names that are not safe to assign and to record how they are used in practice, but attempts to do so have not been successful, and one side effect of the lack of documentation is that any mitigation effect on root name servers or on privacy has been missed.

The document also notes that a domain name can be identified as a DNS name by placing it in the DNS zone or as a Special-Use Domain Name by adding it to the IANA registry, and some names are in both places. At present the only way a name can be added to the registry is for the IETF to take responsibility for it and designate it for technical use, although other potential uses should be recorded in the registry for which the IETF should not take responsibility. In some cases the IETF may need to document that a name is in use without claiming that the use is the IETF's particular use of the name, and no mechanism exists in the current registry to mark names in this way. During the review stages of a document there is no formal process in which a check is made that the document does not unintentionally violate the IETF process for adding names to the registry, as was the case in RFC 7788. Use of the registry is inconsistent: some documents add registry entries and some do not, and some specify how and whether special-use name delegations should be done while others do not. There exists no safe, non-process-violating mechanism for ad hoc assignment of Special-Use Domain Names.

Problems 19 to 21 concern wording and tooling. It is generally assumed that protocols needing a Special-Use Domain Name need a mnemonic, single-label, human-readable name for use in user interfaces such as command lines or URL entry fields, but that assumption is likely not correct in all cases, for example in applications where the domain name is never visible to a user. RFC 6761 uses the term domain name to describe the thing for which special uses are registered, which creates a great deal of confusion because some readers take domain name to imply the use of the DNS protocol. And the use of DNSSEC with Special-Use Domain Names is an open issue, with no consensus or guidance about how to use DNSSEC with the various classes of name; the considerations listed are what class of name is under consideration, whether the name requires a delegation in the root zone and whether that delegation should be signed, what process would let the IETF cause a delegation to be instantiated, and what the recommended practices are for using the DNS with that particular name.
sections.plainLanguage: The problems fall into a few groups: nobody agrees what counts as a technical use, or who has the last word; the process is slow, and people work around it; the process itself is easy to misread or apply wrongly; and there are several names already in use that nobody has ever written down.

sections.title: How Names Reach the Root Today
sections.content:
There are three primary and numerous secondary documents to consider when thinking about the Special-Use Domain Names process. How names are resolved is ambiguous, in the sense that some names are Special-Use Domain Names requiring special handling and some can be resolved using the DNS with no special handling. The assignment of Internet Names is not under the sole control of any one organisation: the IETF has authority in some cases, but only with respect to technical uses, and ICANN is the designated administrator of the root zone but generally not of zones other than the root zone. Neither authority can, in any practical sense, exclude the practice of ad hoc use of names. Unauthorized use of domain names can be accomplished by any entity with control over one or more name servers or resolvers, in the context of any hosts and services it operates, and also by authors of software who decide that a Special-Use Domain Name is the right way to indicate the use of an alternate resolution mechanism.

The primary documents address the IETF's past thinking in a general way and describe what the IETF does in practice. The IAB Technical Comment on the Unique DNS Root is not an IETF consensus document and appears to have been written to address a different problem, but it speaks directly to several key issues and, coming from the IAB, is rightly treated as having significant authority. Its main points relevant here are that the Internet requires a globally unique namespace, in which a given name refers to the same information no matter who requests it and from which name server; that private networks may operate private namespaces with names that have meaning only locally, but names in the public namespace must still be globally unique; that the DNS is not the only protocol that may be used for resolving domain names; and that users cannot be assumed to know how to distinguish symbolic references with local meaning from those with global meaning, so they may share references incorporating domain names with no global meaning. The effect of such a reference escaping the context in which it is valid is that the user's intended communication cannot be understood by the recipients. The same problem occurs when a user copies a name from one context into another, for example copying a .onion domain name out of a Tor browser, where it has meaning, and pasting it into an SSH client that cannot connect over the Tor network. Summarised, the advice is that domain names with unambiguous global meaning are preferable to local names that will be ambiguous, but that both are in use and must be supported, and that there might well be more than one name resolution protocol.

RFC 6761 represents the current IETF consensus on designating and recording Special-Use Domain Names. It defines two aspects: designating a domain name to have a special purpose, and registering that special use in the registry. The designation process is defined in a single sentence, requiring that an IETF Standards Action or IESG Approval specification must be published describing the new functionality, which means any designation is subject to the same open review and consensus process as all other IETF specifications. The registration process is purely mechanical, recording the existence of the newly designated name with a pointer to the section that defines how special handling is to be applied. RFC 6761 provided the process by which Multicast DNS designated .local, and it also enumerated names previously used or defined to have special uses, which could not have been added to the registry because it did not exist before.

Several points follow. A Special-Use Domain Name may be a name that should be resolved using the DNS with no special handling, such as in-addr.arpa, which is not a top-level domain. It may be a name resolved using the DNS that needs no special handling in the stub resolver but does in the recursive resolver, such as 10.in-addr.arpa. It may be a name requiring special handling in the stub resolver, such as .local, which signals that the local stub resolver should use a non-DNS protocol. The current IETF consensus is that all of these purposes are valid. Here the term stub resolver does not mean DNS protocol stub resolver: it is the entity within a software stack that takes a question about a domain name and answers it, and it is there that the decision about which protocol, or which local database, to use is made. RFC 6761 does not limit Special-Use Domain Names to top-level domains, but at present every name in the registry either is intended to be resolved using the DNS, is a top-level domain, or is both.

The Memorandum of Understanding between the IETF and ICANN discusses how names and numbers will be managed through IANA. While it delegates authority for managing the DNS namespace generally to ICANN, it reserves to the IETF the authority that RFC 6761 then formalises, stating that assignments of domain names for technical uses, such as names for inverse DNS lookup, are not considered to be policy issues and remain subject to the provisions of that section of the agreement. Both in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa are in the registry.

The secondary documents show how the process has fared. The July 2001 draft that eventually became the Multicast DNS document designated .local.arpa, which was strongly opposed by working group participants, so the author switched to .local. The .onion top-level domain is important because it is the most recent IETF action on the topic, although it did not set a new policy: the IETF gained consensus to publish it, and devising a resolution was constrained by the absence of an allocation process, so the developers allocated it unilaterally, and by the CA/Browser Forum phasing out certificates for internal names, the IETF's designation was needed to allow a certificate issuance process specific to .onion names. Locally Served DNS Zones describes zones that exist by definition and are resolved using the DNS but cannot have a global meaning because the addresses they reference are not unique, applying to private IPv4 addresses, unique local IPv6 unicast addresses and the shared address space prefix. The document on the discovery of the IPv6 prefix used for address synthesis is an example that successfully used the RFC 6761 process, without controversy or delay, but it did not work correctly: ipv4only.arpa was never added to the registry, because the document did not explicitly request it. And RFC 7788, which defines .home, did not follow the process at all and did not request that .home be added to the registry; this was recognised as a mistake and resulted in an errata report.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for reserving a name say two things: publish a proper specification, and record the name in a central list. The document shows that the second half is easy to forget and sometimes skipped, and that names get used by other people without asking anyone first.

sections.title: How We Got Here
sections.content:
A newcomer may be under the impression that the DNS sprang fully formed directly from Paul Mockapetris' head, as was the birth of Athena in Greek mythology. This is not the case. In the early days of the Internet, hostnames were resolved using a text file, HOSTS.TXT, maintained by a central authority, the Network Information Center, and distributed to all hosts using the File Transfer Protocol. The inefficiency of this process is cited as a reason for the development of the DNS in 1983. The transition from HOSTS.TXT to the DNS was not smooth: Sun Microsystems' Network Information System, at the time known as Yellow Pages, was an active competitor to the DNS, although it failed to provide a complete solution to the global naming problem. Another example was the NetBIOS Name Service, also known as WINS, used mostly by Microsoft Windows machines but also by open-source BSD and Linux operating systems.

Most modern operating systems can still use the /etc/hosts file for name resolution, many still have a name service switch that can be configured on the host to resolve some domains using NIS or WINS, and most have the capability of resolving names using mDNS by recognising the special meaning of .local. The Sun model of having private domains within a corporate site while supporting the global DNS for off-site use persisted even after NIS fell into disuse. Microsoft used to recommend that site administrators use a private top-level domain for internal use, and that practice was very much part of the zeitgeist at the time. This attitude is at the root of the widespread practice of simply picking an apparently unused top-level domain and using it for experimental purposes, which persists at the time of writing.

This history matters because discussions in the IETF often come down to why users of new name resolution protocols choose domain names rather than some other naming concept that does not overlap with the namespace that, in modern times, is by default resolved using the DNS. The answer is that, as a consequence of this long history of resolving domain names using a wide variety of name resolution systems, domain names are required in a large variety of contexts in user interfaces and application programming interfaces. Any name that appears in such a context is a domain name, so developers of new name resolution systems that must work in existing contexts have no choice: they must use a Special-Use Domain Name to segregate a portion of the namespace for use with their system.
sections.plainLanguage: Names were once looked up in a shared text file, and several other systems competed with the DNS before it won. That history is why new protocols end up borrowing a domain name: the name has to fit into places, such as web addresses and command lines, that were built for the DNS.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document mentions various security and privacy considerations in the text, including the operational and privacy effects on root zone servers of queries for names that should have been handled locally, and the use of DNSSEC with Special-Use Domain Names. However, it creates no new security or privacy concerns, and it requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The document raises privacy and stability points as part of its problem list, but it defines nothing that would itself be a security risk.

viz.caption: The twenty-one problems listed in Section 3

items.label: No formal coordination process
items.desc: The IETF and ICANN have a liaison relationship but no formal process for coordinating special-use allocations, which could lead to conflicts.

items.label: No definition of technical use
items.desc: There is no explicit scoping of what can constitute a technical use, and no consensus in the IETF on what the term means.

items.label: Disputed authority
items.desc: Not all protocol developers accept that authority over the entire Domain Namespace should rest with the IETF and ICANN.

items.label: Authority cannot be enforced
items.desc: Neither organisation can stop a third party from using a subset of the namespace, and permissionless innovation is cited as a reason to allow it.

items.label: Ad hoc use happens
items.desc: Organisations use parts of the namespace without following the process, for seven listed reasons including not knowing it exists.

items.label: Several resolution protocols wanted
items.desc: Domain names carry no metadata saying which protocol to use, and resolution APIs give no way to specify one.

items.label: Leakage to root servers
items.desc: Software that does not know a name is special will query the DNS, which is an operational problem for root servers and may reveal private information.

items.label: The process is slow and uncertain
items.desc: Designating .local through the RFC 6761 process took more than ten years, ten times longer than any other part of protocol development.

items.label: Resistance to non-DNS names
items.desc: Seven reasons the IETF resists assigning names to resolution systems outside the DNS, from needing a way to tell which protocol to use to the risk of disputes.

items.label: No fallback process
items.desc: Without an IETF process for technical names, protocols that need such names could not get them.

items.label: The process is misread
items.desc: Assignments have been made treating the suggested considerations as requirements, and de facto assignments have been made outside the process.

items.label: Names in use without due process
items.desc: Several top-level domain names are used for a variety of purposes without due process, and their status needs recording to avoid future disputes.

items.label: Documentation attempts failed
items.desc: The process could document names that are not safe to assign, but attempts have failed, so any mitigation effect on root servers or privacy was missed.

items.label: Only technical uses can be registered
items.desc: The only way in is for the IETF to take responsibility for a name, although other uses should be recorded for which the IETF should not be responsible.

items.label: No way to record a use without claiming it
items.desc: The IETF may need to document that a name is in use without claiming the use is its own, and the registry has no mechanism for that.

items.label: No check during document review
items.desc: There is no formal process to check that a document under review does not unintentionally violate the process for adding names.

items.label: Inconsistent use of the registry
items.desc: Some documents add registry entries and some do not, and some say how delegations should be done while others do not.

items.label: No safe ad hoc route
items.desc: There exists no mechanism for assigning a Special-Use Domain Name ad hoc that does not violate the process.

items.label: Human-readable names assumed
items.desc: It is generally assumed that protocols need a mnemonic single-label name, which is likely not correct when the name is never shown to a user.

items.label: The word domain name confuses
items.desc: RFC 6761 uses the term domain name for what it registers, so some readers take it to imply use of the DNS protocol.

items.label: DNSSEC use is unresolved
items.desc: There is no consensus or guidance on using DNSSEC with the different classes of name, including whether a root delegation should be signed.
